hook.line: Three small words let you say how much: *muy*, *mucho* and *poco*. With them, "I speak Spanish" turns into "I speak a little Spanish", which is the honest version for now.
hook.es: Hablo poco español, pero estudio mucho.
hook.en: I don't speak much Spanish, but I study a lot.

examples.en: I have a lot of questions.
I need a lot of coffee.

rule:
Three jobs, three words.

*muy* = very. It goes before a describing word, and it never changes: *muy bien*, *muy bonito*, *muy despacio*.

*mucho* = a lot, much, many. Before a thing, it matches the thing: *mucho café*, *mucha leche*, *muchos clientes*, *muchas preguntas*.
After a verb, it stays *mucho*: *Tomás habla mucho*.

*poco* = not much, little. It works the same way: *poco pan*, *pocos clientes*, *como poco*.

English uses "very" and "a lot" a bit loosely. Spanish keeps them apart: very good is *muy bueno*, a lot of work is *mucho trabajo*, never *muy trabajo*.
smallPrint: Teachers call these quantifiers: *muy* is an adverb, *mucho* and *poco* agree with the noun they count.

options: There are a lot of arepas.
There's a lot of good bread.
Vale drinks a lot of water.
I have a lot of work.

yourTurn.why: *Bien* describes how you speak, so it takes *muy*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: I need a lot of coffee.

yourTurn.why: *Despacio* says how, so *muy* goes in front.

yourTurn.prompt: Turn it around: Hay muchos clientes hoy. Say there aren't many.
yourTurn.why: *Poco* matches its noun just like *mucho*: *pocos clientes*.

pitfalls.why: *Trabajo* is a thing, and you count things with *mucho*. *Muy* only goes before a describing word.
Very well is *muy bien*. *Mucho* never sits in front of *bien*.
Before a thing, *mucho* takes its ending: *preguntas* needs *muchas*.

personal: Write three true lines about yourself: something you do a lot (*mucho*), something you do a little (*poco*), and something you do very well (*muy bien*).
